73	    >>> events = EventList(time=times, gti=[[0, length]])

82	    >>> lc_renorm.counts = lc.counts / mean
83	    >>> lc_renorm.counts_err = lc.counts_err / mean
84	    >>> lc_renorm.err_dist = "gauss"

87	    >>> get_flux_generator(events, segment_size, dt=None)
88	    Traceback (most recent call last):

326	def _averaged_cospectra_cdf(xcoord, n):
327	    """
328	    Function calculating the cumulative distribution function for
329	    averaged cospectra, Equation 19 of Huppenkothen & Bachetti (2018).
330	
331	    Parameters
332	    ----------
333	    xcoord : float or iterable
334	        The cospectral power for which to calculate the CDF.
335	
336	    n : int
337	        The number of averaged cospectra
338	
339	    Returns
340	    -------
341	    cdf : float
342	        The value of the CDF at `xcoord` for `n` averaged cospectra
343	    """
344	    if np.size(xcoord) == 1:
345	        xcoord = [xcoord]
346	
347	    cdf = np.zeros_like(xcoord)
348	
349	    for i, x in enumerate(xcoord):
350	        prefac_bottom1 = factorial(n - 1)
351	        for j in range(n):
352	            prefac_top = factorial(n - 1 + j)
353	            prefac_bottom2 = factorial(n - 1 - j) * factorial(j)
354	            prefac_bottom3 = 2.0 ** (n + j)
355	
356	            prefac = prefac_top / (prefac_bottom1 * prefac_bottom2 * prefac_bottom3)
357	
358	            gf = -j + n
359	
360	            first_fac = scipy.special.gamma(gf)
361	            if x >= 0:
362	                second_fac = scipy.special.gammaincc(gf, n * x) * first_fac
363	                fac = 2.0 * first_fac - second_fac
364	            else:
365	                fac = scipy.special.gammaincc(gf, -n * x) * first_fac
366	
367	            cdf[i] += prefac * fac
368	        if np.size(xcoord) == 1:
369	            return cdf[i]
370	
371	    return cdf

374	def cospectra_pvalue(power, nspec):
375	    """
376	    This function computes the single-trial p-value that the power was
377	    observed under the null hypothesis that there is no signal in
378	    the data.
379	
380	    Important: the underlying assumption that make this calculation valid
381	    is that the powers in the cross spectrum follow a Laplace distribution,
382	    and this requires that:
383	
384	    1. the co-spectrum is normalized according to [Leahy 1983]_
385	    2. there is only white noise in the light curve. That is, there is no
386	       aperiodic variability that would change the overall shape of the power
387	       spectrum.
388	
389	    Also note that the p-value is for a *single trial*, i.e. the power
390	    currently being tested. If more than one power or more than one power
391	    spectrum are being tested, the resulting p-value must be corrected for the
392	    number of trials (Bonferroni correction).
393	
394	    Mathematical formulation in [Huppenkothen 2017]_.
395	
396	    Parameters
397	    ----------
398	    power :  float
399	        The squared Fourier amplitude of a spectrum to be evaluated
400	
401	    nspec : int
402	        The number of spectra or frequency bins averaged in ``power``.
403	        This matters because averaging spectra or frequency bins increases
404	        the signal-to-noise ratio, i.e. makes the statistical distributions
405	        of the noise narrower, such that a smaller power might be very
406	        significant in averaged spectra even though it would not be in a single
407	        cross spectrum.
408	
409	    Returns
410	    -------
411	    pval : float
412	        The classical p-value of the observed power being consistent with
413	        the null hypothesis of white noise
414	
415	    References
416	    ----------
417	
418	    * .. [Leahy 1983] https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/#abs/1983ApJ...266..160L/abstract
419	    * .. [Huppenkothen 2017] http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJS..236...13H
420	
421	    """
422	    if not np.all(np.isfinite(power)):
423	        raise ValueError("power must be a finite floating point number!")
424	
425	    # if power < 0:
426	    #    raise ValueError("power must be a positive real number!")
427	
428	    if not np.isfinite(nspec):
429	        raise ValueError("nspec must be a finite integer number")
430	
431	    if not np.isclose(nspec % 1, 0):
432	        raise ValueError("nspec must be an integer number!")
433	
434	    if nspec < 1:
435	        raise ValueError("nspec must be larger or equal to 1")
436	
437	    elif nspec == 1:
438	        lapl = scipy.stats.laplace(0, 1)
439	        pval = lapl.sf(power)
440	
441	    elif nspec > 50:
442	        exp_sigma = np.sqrt(2) / np.sqrt(nspec)
443	        gauss = scipy.stats.norm(0, exp_sigma)
444	        pval = gauss.sf(power)
445	
446	    else:
447	        pval = 1.0 - _averaged_cospectra_cdf(power, nspec)
448	
449	    return pval

1223	        number of powers averaged in each bin.

1226	        following underlying assumptions are fulfilled:
1227

1229	        2. There is no source of variability in the data other than the
1230	           periodic signal to be determined with this method. This is important!
1231	           If there are other sources of (aperiodic) variability in the data, this
1232	           method will *not* produce correct results, but instead produce a large
1233	           number of spurious false positive detections!
1234	        3. There are no significant instrumental effects changing the
1235	           statistical distribution of the powers (e.g. pile-up or dead time)
1236	
1237	        By default, the method produces ``(index,p-values)`` for all powers in
1238	        the power spectrum, where index is the numerical index of the power in
1239	        question. If a ``threshold`` is set, then only powers with p-values
1240	        *below* that threshold with their respective indices. If
1241	        ``trial_correction`` is set to ``True``, then the threshold will be corrected
1242	        for the number of trials (frequencies) in the power spectrum before
1243	        being used.

1245	        Parameters
1246	        ----------
1247	        threshold : float, optional, default ``1``
1248	            The threshold to be used when reporting p-values of potentially
1249	            significant powers. Must be between 0 and 1.
1250	            Default is ``1`` (all p-values will be reported).
1251

1253	            A Boolean flag that sets whether the ``threshold`` will be corrected
1254	            by the number of frequencies before being applied. This decreases
1255	            the ``threshold`` (p-values need to be lower to count as significant).

1785	        a constant dead time for all events.
1786	        For more advanced dead time corrections, see the FAD method from `stingray.deadtime.fad`
1787

1789	        ----------
1790	        dead_time: float

1796	        ----------------

1799	            combination of the source counts and background counts (e.g. in an imaging X-ray detector).
1800	        paralyzable: bool, default False

1802	            dead time. If False, the correction is done assuming a non-paralyzable
1803	            (more common) dead time.

1806	            calculations. Check the plots returned by  the `check_B` and
1807	            `check_A` functions to test that this number is adequate.

1823	            raise NotImplementedError("Paralyzable dead time correction is not implemented yet.")

1826	            self.freq,
1827	            dead_time,

1829	            bin_time=self.dt,

187	We define $s^2 \equiv |\left<S_1^*S_2\right>|^2$, $a^2 \equiv
188	|\left<C\right>|^2$, and 
189	$n^2 \equiv (|S_1|^2|N_2|^2+|N_1|^2|S_2|^2+|N_1|^2|N_2|^2)/m$. 
190	The probability distribution of the measured cross spectrum, 
191	$|\left<C\right>|^2$,  given an intrinsic cross spectrum and Poisson noise,
192	is equivalent to the distribution of total power in an individual frequency
193	bin of a noisy power spectrum; it is given by
194	\be
195	p(a^2|s^2,n^2)~=~{n^{-2}}\exp\left[{{-(a^2+s^2)} \over {n^2}}\right]
196	               I_0\left({{2as} \over {n^2}}\right)
197	\label{p(a)}
198	\ee
199	(Groth 1975, Goodman 1985), where $I_0$ is the zero order Bessel function of
200	the first kind.  This can be inverted to yield the probability distribution
201	of $s^2$ given a measured cross spectrum and Poisson noise,
202	\be
203	p(s^2|a^2,n^2)={{(ns)^{-2}}\over{\sqrt{\pi}}}
204	                \exp\left[{{-(a^2+2s^2)} \over {2n^2}}\right]
205	{{I_0({{2as}/{n^2}})}\over{{I_0({{a^2}/{2n^2}})}}} .
206	\label{p(s2)}
207	\ee
208	(Chakrabarty 1996).  For $a\gg n$, equation~\ref{p(a)} can be 
209	approximated by the Gaussian
210	\be
211	p(a^2|s^2,n^2) ~\approx~ {1 \over {2na\sqrt{\pi}}}
212	\exp\left[{{-(a-s)^2} \over {n^2}}\right],
213	\label{approx-p(s)}
214	\ee
215	in which case $\left<a^2\right>=\left<s^2\right>+\left<n^2\right>$ and
216	$\delta a^2=\sqrt{2}n^2$.  
217	The intrinsic coherence can be usefully estimated when the
218	following conditions are met: $s\gtsim n$,
219	$|S_1|^2/|N_1|^2\gtsim1/\sqrt{m}$, and $|S_2|^2/|N_2|^2\gtsim1/\sqrt{m}$.
220	
221	The following is a recipe for estimating the value and uncertainty of
222	the intrinsic coherence from measurements of $\left<C\right>$, $P_1$ and $P_2$.
223	Average powers and cross spectra should be constructed from unnormalized
224	measurements.  In practice it will often be necessary to correct the 
225	Poisson noise level for instrumental dead time (cf. van der Klis 1989 for
226	a detailed discussion).  Dead time can introduce correlations between
227	energy channels that enhance or diminish coherence.  These are intrument
228	dependent and beyond the scope of this Letter.  The terms high power
229	and high measured coherence used below denote powers that satisy 
230	$|S|^2$ greater than a few times $|N|^2/\sqrt{m}$ 
231	in each channel and measured coherence that satisfies
232	$\gamma^2$ greater than a few times $n^2/(P_1P_2)$, respectively.
233	In many cases, these conditions will be
234	satisfied at some frequencies but not at others.
235	
236	\smallskip
237	{\sl High powers, high measured coherence.---} 
238	\bea
239	\gamma_I^2 &=& { {|\left<C\right>|^2-n^2} \over {|S_1|^2|S_2|^2} }
240	     \Bigg ( 1~\pm~ m^{-1/2} \Bigg [~ { {2n^4 m} \over 
241	     {(|\left<C\right>|^2-n^2)^2 } }
242	     \nonumber \\
243	     &+& { {|N_1|^4} \over {|S_1|^4} } + { {|N_2|^4} \over {|S_2|^4} } +
244	     { {m \delta \gamma_I^2} \over {\gamma_I^4} } ~ \Bigg ]^{1/2} ~ \Bigg )
245	     ~~.
246	\label{gamma-high}
247	\eea
248	This is the Gaussian limit, and in essence it corresponds to optimally
249	filtering the measured coherence.  The first three terms in the uncertainty
250	come from uncertainties in Poisson noise, and the last term is from the
251	statistical uncertainty in the intrinsic coherence.
252	
253	\smallskip
254	{\sl High powers, low measured coherence.---}Use 
255	equation~(\ref{p(s2)}) to determine
256	confidence limits, $|\left<S_1^*S_2\right>|^2_{\rm min}$ and 
257	$|\left<S_1^*S_2\right>|^2_{\rm max}$,
258	on $|\left<S_1^*S_2\right>|^2$.  Confidence limits on $\gamma^2_I$ are
259	then 
260	\be
261	\gamma^2_{I,{{\rm max} \atop {\rm min}}} = 
262	     { { |\left<S_1^*S_2\right>|^2_{{\rm max} \atop {\rm min}} }
263	     \over  { |S_1|^2 |S_2|^2 } }
264	     \left ( 1 \pm \sqrt{ { {|N_1|^4} \over {m|S_1|^4} } 
265	     + { {|N_2|^4} \over {m|S_2|^4} }  
266	     + { { \delta \gamma_I^2 } \over {\gamma_I^4} } }  \right ) ~.
267	\ee
268	
269	
270	\smallskip
271	{\sl Low powers.---}This difficult case
272	arises in weak sources and at high frequency.  In practice the $1\sigma$
273	errors in this case are likely to extend nearly from 0 to 1.  The authors
274	do not know a closed form for $p(\gamma_I^2)$.  We recommend using
275	equation~(\ref{p(s2)}) and the Gaussian probability distributions of 
276	$|S_1|^2$ and $|S_2|^2$ to emperically map out $p(\gamma_I^2)$ and 
277	determine confidence limits on the intrinsic coherence.
278	
279	
280	
281	\section{Examples of Incoherent Sources}
282	
283	\smallskip
284	\noindent{\sl Thermal Flares.---} Let us imagine that the observed variability
285	is completely the result of local temperature fluctuations with some time
286	dependence, $T(t)$, which can be arbitrarily complicated so long as it is
287	statistically stationary.  Let the intrinsic time series, $s_1(t)$ and
288	$s_2(t)$, be photon count rates in narrow frequency bands $(\nu_1, \nu_1 +
289	\delta \nu_1)$ and $(\nu_2, \nu_2 + \delta \nu_2)$.  The observed count
290	rate in frequency band 1 is approximately proportional to $\nu_1^2 \delta
291	\nu_1 \left ( \exp \left [ {{h \nu_1}/{kT(t)}} \right ] ~-~ 1 \right )^{-1}
292	$, and likewise for energy band 2.  If both $h\nu_1$ and $h \nu_2 \ll k
293	T(t)$, then we are on the Rayleigh-Jeans portion of the spectrum, in which 
294	case $s_1(t) \propto s_2(t) \propto T(t)$.  Thus there is a linear transfer
295	function (a constant) between the two channels, and therefore the coherence
296	function will be unity. On the other hand, if $kT(t) \ll h \nu_1$ and $h
297	\nu_2$, then we are on the Wien tail of the spectrum, in which case we have
298	$s_2(t) \propto s_1(t)^{(\nu_2/\nu_1)} \propto \exp[-h \nu_2/kT(t)]$.  
299	Thus there is a nonlinear transfer function.  In general, such a transfer 
300	function will take power from a frequency $f$ and distribute it among 
301	harmonics of $f$ (cf. Bendat \& Piersol 1986) and therefore lead to a loss of 
302	coherence.
303	
304	\smallskip
305	\noindent{\sl Multiple Flaring Regions.---}A number of models for X-ray
306	variability in Galactic black hole candidates associate different
307	timescales with different physical regions of an accretion disk (cf. Nowak
308	1994, Miyamoto et al. 1994).  If more than one region contributes to the
309	signal in both energy bands, then it is possible for the coherence function
310	to be less than unity, even if {\it individual} regions produce
311	perfectly coherent variability.
312	
313	Consider two flaring regions: one produces a time series $q(t) = q_1(t) +
314	q_2(t)$, and the other produces a time series $r(t) = r_1(t) +
315	r_2(t)$---each in energy bands 1 and 2, respectively.  Furthermore, 
316	assume that there
317	is a constant linear transfer function that relates $q_1(t)$ to $q_2(t)$,
318	as well as another constant, linear transfer function that relates $r_1(t)$ to
319	$r_2(t)$, with $q_1(t)$ and $r_1(t)$ otherwise being completely uncorrelated.
320	Denoting the intrinsic time series observed in band 1 as
321	$s_1(t) = q_1(t) + r_1(t)$, and the intrinsic time series observed in band
322	2 as $s_2(t) = q_2(t) + r_2(t)$, the intrinsic coherence function between
323	the two bands is then 
324	\be
325	\gamma^2_I = {{ Q_1^2 Q_2^2 + R_1^2 R_2^2 + 2 
326	     | Q_1 | | Q_2 | | R_1 | | R_2 |  \cos ( \delta \theta_r - \delta
327	     \theta_q  ) } \over { Q_1^2 Q_2^2 + R_1^2 R_2^2 + Q_1^2 R_2^2 + 
328	     Q_2^2 R_1^2 }} ,
329	\label{multi_coh}
330	\ee
331	where $\delta \theta_q$ and $\delta \theta_r$ are the mean Fourier phase
332	differences between $Q_1(f)$ and $Q_2(f)$ and between $R_1(f)$ and
333	$R_2(f)$, respectively.   (The quantities on the right hand side of 
334	equation (\ref{multi_coh}) refer to their mean values.)
335	One can easily show that for this case $\gamma^2_I \le 1$, and is only
336	equal to unity if both $\delta \theta_q = \delta \theta_r$ and $| Q_1 |/|
337	Q_2 | = | R_1 |/| R_2 |$.  That is to say, the coherence function is unity 
338	{\it if and only if} the same linear transfer function that takes $q_1(t)$ 
339	to $q_2(t)$ also takes $r_1(t)$ to $r_2(t)$.
340	
341	
342	\section{Examples of Coherent Sources}
343	
344	
345	Here we present an idealized model that produces unity coherence while
346	producing phase lags qualitatively similar to those seen in Cyg X--1
347	(i.e. phase lags approximately independent of Fourier frequency; Miyamoto
348	et al. 1992).  Imagine that we have a disk with a stochastic source of 
349	(linear) surface density perturbations at the center that propagate
350	outwards at some constant speed $c_s$.  If we take the source to be given
351	by $(4 \pi r)^{-1} \delta(r) \sigma_s(t)$, then the resultant surface
352	density perturbations---$\sigma_p(r, t)$, at radius $r$ and time $t$ 
353	(using the two-dimensional wave propagation Green's function; cf. Morse \& 
354	Feschbach 1953)---are given by
355	\be
356	\sigma_p (r,t) ~=~ \int dt' ~\sigma_s(t') ~ {{\theta[~ (t-t') ~-~ r/c_s ~]}
357	 \over {\sqrt{~ (t-t')^2 ~-~ r^2/c_s^2 ~} } } ~~,
358	\label{two_d}
359	\ee
360	where $\theta$ is the step function.   Let the fluctuating signal in 
361	band 1, $s_1(t)$, be equal to the surface density perturbation times 
362	a weighting function, $g_1(r)$, integrated over the
363	entire disk.  The radially integrated Green's function is just a linear
364	transfer function, thus the Fourier transform of $s_1(t)$ becomes
365	\be
366	S_1(f) ~=~ \Sigma_s(f) ~ \int i 2 \pi^2 ~r g_1(r) ~ H_0^{(1)} \left (
367	     {{2 \pi |f| r}\over{c_s}} \right ) ~dr 
368	     ~~,
369	\label{two_dtrans}
370	\ee 
371	which we define as $\Sigma_s (f) T_1 (f)$, and where
372	$H_0^{(1)}(x)$ is the Hankel function of $x$ as well as the Fourier transform
373	of the two-dimensional Green's function.  Similarly we have 
374	$S_2(f)\equiv \Sigma_s(f) T_2 (f)$.  As both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are linearly 
375	related to the source $\Sigma_s$, there is a linear transfer function 
376	equal to $T_2/T_1$ that takes $S_1$ to $S_2$, and therefore there is unity 
377	coherence.  We could write such a transfer function only because the
378	driving source was separable in time and space (in this case being 
379	spatially localized).
380	
381	Equation (\ref{two_dtrans}) is analytically tractable if we set $g_1(r) =
382	\exp(-\alpha_1 r/r_0 )$ and $g_2(r) = \exp(-\alpha_2 r/r_0)$, as one might
383	have for weighting functions representing flux from a Wien tail.  As will
384	be discussed elsewhere (Vaughan et al. 1997), the resulting time lags are
385	qualitatively similar to those seen in Cyg X--1.  We require $r_0/c_s
386	\sim 1$ to obtain quantitative agreement with the observations, which
387	implies an extremely slow propagation speed, $c_s \sim 10^{-4} c$.  This
388	mechanism is qualitatively similar to that proposed by Manmoto et
389	al. (1996), where thermal waves are launched from large disk radii toward
390	the center, and then reflect from the disk inner edge as acoustic waves.
391	However, the mechanism of Manmoto et al. (1996) cannot preserve coherence
392	if, as in the example of \S3, there are multiple, spatially distributed
393	source functions ({\it in the X-ray-emitting regions}) for the waves.
394	Furthermore, the acoustic waves shock upon reflection, which is an
395	inherently non-linear process that also will lead to a loss of coherence,
396	if emission from the reflected shock is an appreciable fraction of the
397	total observed emission.
398	
399	Adding additional mechanisms in the form of successive transfer functions
400	will lead to unity coherence so long as each component is itself linear.
401	In the above example, we could have invoked Comptonization as a subsequent
402	transfer mechanism, which would have introduced additional time delays.  So
403	long as the Compton cloud is static, coherence will be preserved (cf. Nowak
404	\& Vaughan 1996). 
405	
406	
407	\section{Observational Examples}
408	
409	
410	Of the above physical situations where coherence is preserved and those
411	where it is not, which cases are observed in nature?  Surprisingly, the
412	answer seems to be that unity coherence is the norm, despite the variety of
413	ways of weakening coherence.  Here we present two black hole candidates:
414	GX339--4 in its very high state, and Cyg X--1 in its low state.  Both
415	have been modeled with disks plus Compton coronae (cf. Miyamoto et
416	al. 1991; Dove, Wilms, \& Begelman 1996 and references therein), although
417	there are differences between them:  the very high state has a substantial
418	soft ($\sim 1$ keV) component, the low state has none;  the hard tail of
419	the very high state is softer than the hard tail of the low state ($\sim
420	2.5$ photon index compared to $\sim 1.7$);  the very high state has lower
421	variability (rms $\sim 10-20\%$) than the low state (rms $\sim 40\%$).
422	Yet, as shown in Figure 1, both systems apparently have unity intrinsic
423	coherence, at least between low energies and at low frequency.
424	
425	Figure 1 presents coherence plots derived from {\it Ginga} data.  
426	The methods described above have been used to
427	filter the noise from the data. Poisson noise and uncertainties in the
428	{\it Ginga} dead time make the coherence estimates unreliable 
429	above $\sim 10$ Hz ; however, at frequencies below 10~Hz the
430	intrinsic coherence is essentially unity.  This result holds true for Cyg
431	X--1 over a wide range of energy channels.  On the other hand, the GX 339--4
432	variability (the PSD is shown as Fig. {\it 4b} in Miyamoto et al. 1991) shows
433	unity coherence between low energies but shows a dramatic drop in
434	coherence between the $2.3-4.6$ keV and $13.9-37.1$ keV channels.
435	
436	Considering the mechanisms discussed above, this loss of coherence is not
437	surprising. Perhaps the $13.9-37.1$ keV band corresponds to a Wien tale,
438	and, therefore, to a nonlinear transfer function. It is more difficult to
439	explain the observed unity coherence.  We expect that most shot models
440	(cf. Lochner et al. 1991) will produce less than unity coherence.  For
441	example, the kinematic model of Nowak (1994) for the very high state of GX
442	339--4 successfully reproduced the observed PSDs and phase lags. However,
443	as the viscous and thermal fluctuations were distributed over a large range
444	of radii and overlapped in time, the mechanism led to less than unity
445	coherence (not shown in that paper) between {\it all} energy bands.  In
446	order to preserve coherence, we always require linear responses, and we
447	usually require the following: localized sources and/or localized
448	responses; a (temporally) uniform source throughout the disk; or a uniform
449	response throughout the disk.  Most of these features are absent from
450	current models.
451	
452	The data described above will be presented in greater detail in Vaughan et
453	al. (1997).  Here we have presented them to demonstrate that there are
454	observational and, by extension, physical differences between the systems,
455	despite the fact that they are both commonly fit with coronae models.  The
456	coherence function therefore offers us another tool to help distinguish
457	among theoretical models.
458	
459	
460	
461	\section{Conclusions}
462	
463	
464	We have described a statistic, the coherence function, that is derivable
465	from the cross spectrum used to compute phase or time lags between two
466	times series.  This statistic has traditionally been ignored; however, it
467	contains additional information about the system, and the methods described
468	above can minimize the noise effects.  Whenever one calculates the phase
469	lag, one can and should also calculate the coherence function.
470	
471	In general, coherence will be lost whenever there is a nonlinear transfer
472	function between two channels, or whenever there are multiple, uncorrelated
473	(linear or nonlinear) transfer functions between two channels.  However, our
474	experience has been that coherence is preserved more often than
475	not.  This is a challenge for theoretical models, as there are many more
476	mechanisms for destroying coherence than there are for preserving
477	coherence.
478	
479	We presented data from two black hole candidates: GX 339--4 in its very high
480	state and Cyg X--1 in its low state.  At low frequency and low energy both
481	preserve coherence, although GX 339--4 loses coherence between high- and
482	low-energy bands.  Theoretical models have addressed observations of phase
483	and time lags (cf. Nowak 1994, Manmoto et al. 1996, etc.), as measured with
484	{\it EXOSAT}, {\it Ginga}, and other X-ray timing instruments. No model 
485	currently accounts for the coherence properties detected in GX 339--4 and 
486	Cyg X--1.  Forthcoming {\it RXTE} observations, however, coupled with the 
487	tools presented above, can help provide new insights into the physical 
488	mechanisms at work in these systems, as well as new challenges for
489	theorists to meet.
